newsitem.title: USA: FOCUS-Greater LME openness offers COMEX few crumbs.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Greater LME openness offers COMEX few crumbs.

text.p: As the London Metal Exchange rings in post-Sumitomo changes to shed light on its inner workings, New York's rival Commodity Exchange Inc (COMEX) needs other ways to boost volumes than a more regulated competitor, traders and analysts said.

"I think the LME is the mature market and the additional information is unlikely to alter that pattern," William O'Neill, senior futures strategist at Merrill Lynch, said. "The LME will continue to do the same level of volumes."
On Thursday LME CEO David King said it was crucial that injecting more transparency into how the exchange operates was handled sensibly so as not to drive business away.

Behind his regulatory juggling act lay some trader fears that if LME becomes as transparent as COMEX is under U.S. trading rules, some players may shy away from the extra scrutiny while others may feel there is no disadvantage using COMEX.
Traders have said they avoid COMEX because it is too regulated and too thinly traded.
The LME is considering telling the market if a player - which would not be named - held a long or short position above say 20 percent.
A large warehouse position could be reported in a similar way, King said.
Both COMEX and LME trade copper contracts, a market which LME dominates, as in zinc, aluminum and other metals.
"Where else are people going to go - there is no other place to trade zinc and so on," a broker at one LME ring dealing member company said.
"The only people being scared off as those that want to do something shady. People trade on LME for other reasons than the lack of transparency," the broker added.
Fred Demler of E D and F Man International disagreed.
"You can have legitimate users who do not want the market to know what they are doing," Demler said.
For instance, an aluminum company shutting for maintenance may need to buy large amounts of metal to meet customer orders, a move which may hamper the hedging strategy if disclosed, Demler said.
And even if a company's name was not published alongside the position data, it would be impossible to keep it secret.
"It's hard to hide a 20 percent position in the metals market," Demler said.

But even if COMEX fails to grab more business because of greater transparency on LME, some believe that a market-maker proposal aired by Patrick Thompson, president of NYMEX, of which COMEX is a division, could generate more volume.

Thompson told Reuters during Copper Club week the exchange was exploring a "market-maker" program allowing selected, highly-capitalised market-makers to take on a requirement to make markets on COMEX in copper and even aluminum, and trade minimum volumes.
For the big LME ring dealers market-making on COMEX would be a natural progression from their LME activities, and would simplify arbitrage trading, a broker said.
"All the large players on LME would probably extend that to COMEX, but what might happen is that it could make things tough for the local traders in New York," he added.

And ironically, as the LME soldiers on to greater transparency, a bill proposed by Senators Richard Lugar and Tom Harkin, is gaining momentum in the U.S. which would strip the CFTC of much of its regulatory authority over the domestic futures industry.

Oversight of futures trading by professionals, which accounts for the vast majority of U.S. futures turnover, would effectively by eliminated, a step which could boost trading volumes, observers have said.
But O'Neill cautioned, "In commodities, not just copper, once a market is established as the dominant one, it's very difficult to switch that pattern of trading to another market."
NYMEX is also looking to boost volumes via expanding its ACCESS electronic trading system in Asia, and a possible second COMEX copper contract once a warehouse is opened in Chile.
